task: Has a way to get official updates without power: a battery or hand-crank radio, a charged phone, or alerts turned on.
why: Warnings, warming or cooling centers and restoration times come through official channels.

task: Uses the warning time: charges phones and batteries, fills water containers, and gets cash and fuel if a long outage is likely.
why: Power, water pressure and card payments can all fail once the outage starts.

task: Uses flashlights rather than candles, and keeps warm without any fuel-burning heater, stove or generator indoors.
why: Candles cause house fires during outages, and indoor combustion causes carbon monoxide poisoning.

task: Runs the generator only outdoors, well away from doors, windows and vents, and never in a garage.
why: Generator exhaust kills quickly, even in a garage with the door open.

task: Checks that a battery carbon monoxide detector is working, and knows the symptoms (headache, dizziness, nausea).
why: Carbon monoxide has no smell, and outages are when people improvise heat.

task: Keeps the refrigerator and freezer closed, and knows when perishable food must be thrown out.
why: A closed refrigerator keeps food cold for about 4 hours; food held above 40 °F for more than 2 hours isn't safe.

task: Moves refrigerated medication into a cooler with ice packs, keeps it from freezing, and checks its temperature.
why: Many refrigerated medications lose potency outside their storage range, whether too warm or frozen.

task: Works out how long the medical device can run on backup power, and decides early where to go before it runs out.
why: Waiting until the battery is nearly empty leaves no time to travel safely.

task: Gathers everyone in one room, closes it off, covers windows and dresses in layers.
why: Heating less space keeps people warmer for longer without any heat source.

task: Protects pipes (dripping taps, open cabinet doors) and knows where the main water shutoff is.
why: A burst pipe floods the home and cuts off water just when it's hardest to get help.

task: Tracks stored water against 1 gallon per person per day, and has a plan if it runs low.
why: Water runs out faster than people expect, and pumps and treatment can fail in long outages.

task: Checks on neighbors, especially older people living alone, without putting the household at risk.
why: Isolated older adults are among those most at risk in extended outages.

task: Saves phone battery and agrees how the household will stay in touch with family if networks fail.
why: Cell networks overload or lose power; a written contact list and a check-in plan still work.

task: Keeps pets warm or cool, fed and watered, and limits time outdoors in extreme weather.
why: Animals are vulnerable to the same temperature extremes, and stressed pets may bolt.

task: Plans for the person with a breathing condition: enough inhalers or medication, and avoiding cold air, smoke or heat triggers.
why: Cold air, smoke and heat are common triggers, and pharmacies may be closed.

task: Sets a clear point at which the household will leave (indoor temperature, supplies, health), and where it will go.
why: Deciding in advance avoids leaving too late, when travel is harder and people are weaker.

task: Has a plan for hygiene and toilets if water stops, and keeps hands and food areas clean.
why: Sanitation failures cause illness in long outages.

task: Counts remaining medication against how long the emergency may last, and contacts a pharmacy or prescriber before running out.
why: Running out of daily medication mid-emergency can quickly become a medical emergency.

task: Keeps routines and reassurance going for children, and explains what's happening at their level.
why: Children cope better with structure and honest, calm explanations.
